articles.title: Former England football star Shaun Wright-Phillips joins Strictly 2026 line-up
articles.text:
Former England and Manchester City winger Shaun Wright-Phillips is the latest star to join the line-up for this year's Strictly Come Dancing.

The football pundit, who is the son of Arsenal legend Ian Wright, had 36 caps for England and also played for clubs including Chelsea and Queens Park Rangers.

His fancy footwork may have dazzled on the pitch but Wright-Phillips says this latest challenge "is definitely outside my comfort zone. Dancing is in my blood -but mainly at family events! I'm super excited to get started and really looking forward to the challenge!"

While ex-footballers have had mixed fortunes on previous Strictly series, former soccer star Karen Carney flipped the script last year by winning the coveted glitterball.

Wright-Phillips is the tenth celebrity to be confirmed for this year's series, joining stars including Delta Goodrem, Lacey Turner, Dani Dyer and Jaime Winstone.

More celebrities are set to be announced in the coming weeks, with 15 expected in the final line-up.

Scroll down to see the rest of this year's line-up so far:

Antonia has portrayed dragon-rider Lady Baela Targaryen in HBO's Game of Thrones prequel since 2022. She is currently starring as Eurydice in the Tony Award-winning musical Hadestown in London's West End.

Her acting career began when she was 14 when she appeared in a short film adaptation of The Tempest, before being cast as a guest role in the BBC's Doctors.

The singer and actress has also appeared in series including Nolly, Stay Close, Stath Lets Flats, and Doctor Who.

Antonia said: "I can't quite believe that I will be heading to the Strictly ballroom this September! I have grown up watching Strictly, and I am so excited to take the challenge on and (hopefully!) learn a new skill. See you on the dancefloor!"

Jaime Winstone launched her acting career in 2004 and her film credits include Bullet Boy, Tomb Raider and Wild Bill, as well stage productions such as 2:22 A Ghost Story.

The actress, who also won acclaim for her portrayal of Barbara Windsor in the BBC biopic Babs, said she was "so excited" to be joining the dance competition.

The actress said in a statement she was "no stranger to a dance floor", but added that ballroom is "a whole new world for me".

"I love a challenge though," she continued, "so can't wait to enter my showgirl era and get super sparkly!"

Winstone has also appeared in TV series such as Poirot, Dead Set, Torvill & Dean, Mad Dogs, Count Abdulla and Four Lives.

After playing Windsor in Babs, Winstone stepped into the late actress's famous role of Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders, appearing in flashback specials, most recently in the soap's 40th anniversary last year.

Known as Great Britain's most successful Paralympian of all time, Dame Sarah Storey has secured 19 gold medals across the nine Paralympic Games she competed in.

The swimmer and cyclist said embarking on the challenge is "hugely exciting" and she "can't wait to get started".

"I have always loved watching Strictly and my daughter Louisa is a very talented dancer, so to be able to learn from the best and hopefully understand even more about her world, is incredibly motivating!" she said.

The former athlete won four golds at London 2012. She started her career as a swimmer and later switched to cycling, winning 30 Paralympic medals in total.

Best is known for hosting Big Brother with AJ Odudu on ITV since 2023, and as host of the Hits Radio Breakfast Show alongside Fleur East and James Barr.

He said it was "an absolute dream" to be taking to the BBC One contest's dance floor in September, "albeit a pretty terrifying one".

Best added: "I've been lucky to do lots of live telly before, but absolutely nothing like this. And I cannot wait!

"I have no idea if I can actually dance, but bring on the sequins, bring on the quicksteps, bring on the dance floor! I'm going to try to enjoy every minute of it."

Mercer was part of the winning couple on ITV dating show Love Island last year, and also works as a model and DJ, and is an ambassador for a young people's mental health charity.

"I have grown up watching the show with my family and am so excited to now be part of the cast," he said.

Mercer also showcases his Afrobeat, hip-hop and street dance moves on his social media accounts.

"Dancing is a huge passion of mine and I can't wait to learn ballroom and do the foxtrot for the first time!" he added.

Delta Goodrem is also part of this year's celebrity list, with the Australian singer and actress becoming the third celebrity to be announced for the upcoming series.

"I've been incredibly honoured to perform on many different stages throughout my career - from TV, theatre, film sets, to touring my own shows around the world," Goodrem said.

"There is, however, one stage I've never stepped onto and that is the ballroom floor. I'm absolutely thrilled to be joining Strictly and can't wait to get started."

She rose to fame in hit Australian soap opera Neighbours and recently represented her nation in the 2026 edition of the Eurovision Song Contest.

Celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton is also part of this year's line-up.

Appleton, best known for his work with Kim Kardashian, joins singer-songwriter Delta Goodrem, EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and reality star Dani Dyer in the battle for the Glitterball trophy.

The Leicester-born Color Wow creative director said: "I'm thrilled to be joining Strictly Come Dancing and coming home to the UK for this incredible experience."

He has also created red carpet looks for the likes of Jennifer Lopez, Katy Perry and Ariana Grande, while having his work showcased on the covers of publications including Vogue, Harper's Bazaar and Vanity Fair.

"I've always believed that the best things happen when you take a chance and try something new," added the 43-year-old, who this year released a memoir entitled Your Roots Don't Define You.

"I may know my way around a salon floor, but the dance floor is a whole different story - and I can't wait to get started."

Lacey Turner was the first contestant to be announced for this year's series, which is expected to begin in September.

She said she was "so excited to be making my way to the dance floor", adding that she was a "huge fan" of the show.

Turner, 38, is best known for her role as Stacey Slater on the BBC One soap, which she joined in 2004.

She has won a British Soap Award and National Television Award for her role, and has also starred in TV dramas including the BBC's Our Girl.

In a video posted on Instagram, Turner said she was "so excited and so terrified at the same time" to be taking part in the show.

"But I've had so many friends do Strictly, and I thought it was about time that I pluck up the courage and made my way on to the dance floor."

Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe will take over as Strictly presenters this year, following the departures of Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.

The first line-up announcements were made significantly earlier than usual - the BBC usually confirms the line-up in August.

Speaking to ITV's Good Morning Britain in June, Ballas said: "There are going to be some people on there that will make you go 'wow'."

Asked about the new presenting trio, Ballas said she was "very excited to see what they bring" to the show.

"I know they took lots of chemistry tests, as did everybody, and those chemistry tests have brought those three people together, and I believe it's absolutely unbelievable," she said.

Ballas described the number of new elements on this year's show as "quite extraordinary", but added that it will still feel familiar to viewers.

"I don't think they'll change the show too much, maybe tweaks here and there, but no major changes."

Ballas, Craig Revel Horwood, Motsi Mabuse and Anton Du Beke will all return as judges.

Regular pro dancers including Amy Dowden, Dianne Buswell, Katya Jones, Vito Coppola and Aljaz Skorjanec will all be back on the dance floor.

However, professional dancers Gorka Marquez, Nadiya Bychkova, Luba Mushtuk, Karen Hauer and Michelle Tsiakkas will not be returning this year.

articles.title: Spider-Man VFX actor trained for Brand New Day role all his life
articles.text:
For Teifion Sussex, playing Spider-Man was something he'd trained for his entire life.

Using YouTube tutorials, he would spend his time in his Somerset home learning parkour and martial arts moves, in the hope he would be called into action one day.

Fast forward to 2026, and the 36-year-old can be seen on the big screen in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, as the VFX, motion-captured double of the titular hero.

He said he spent his childhood pulling the Spidey poses and shooting webs, and now being able to portray him is "the best feeling ever".

Now living near Shepton Mallet, Sussex said his childhood was filled with "driving my parents nuts with my energy", and constantly "throwing myself over furniture and jumping on things".

And it was this upbringing that led to him carving a path as voice actor and physical performer.

So while Tom Holland, the actor behind the current incarnation of Spider-Man, was filming his scenes around the UK - including places like Dorchester Prison in Dorset - Sussex was locked on a sound stage, known as The Volume, throwing shapes to hundreds of cameras.

"Everything was always under a code name," he said, adding: "You don't really 100% know you're working on something until you're actually there doing it."

Sussex said until he looked up and saw the small screen capturing him - he had no idea he was performing on behalf of the friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man.

"Every single little tiny movement you do gets picked up and it gets transferred directly into the character on screen," he added.

"It shows a pre-rendered live capture ... and when I looked up at the screen, and I saw Spider-Man looking back at me - it was like a mirror.

"That was when I realised this is real - this is really happening.

"I was realising this was the real deal. It wasn't a spinoff, it wasn't a fan project or a promotional thing - It was the movie and they needed my help to bring his action to life with my skills and performance.

"That's indescribable really."

He added every day since discovering his role, he had "woken up and it's felt like an actual dream".

Motion capture, or MoCap, is when an actor wears a special suit covered in dots or balls to physically act out scenes, which can then be overlayed on to an animated or digitally generated character.

Oscar De Mello, who helps run The Shed in Bristol which uses MoCap technology, said being one of those performers was a unique skillset, often having to use bigger, more exaggerated movements.

"It enables things that wouldn't otherwise be possible - Motion capture isn't necessarily cheap, it's probably got more affordable as the process has become more efficient but you still need to do it in a studio because you need controlled conditions.

"It is a tool that can be used in a number of different ways for different objectives, and it can enable you to create shots within a TV show or a film that would otherwise be impractical to try and get."

And for Sussex, this meant getting Spider-Man swinging through New York - or battling the Incredible Hulk.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran: Singer to expand his foundation's work to island of Ireland
articles.text:
The musician Ed Sheeran is to expand his foundation's work into the island of Ireland.

The Ed Sheeran Foundation is initially funding North South Sounds 2026, which is bringing 50 young musicians from Belfast and Cork together.

Young people aged 13-17 from the Oh Yeah Centre in Belfast have worked alongside young people from Music Generation in Cork.

They are due to perform gigs at the Oh Yeah Centre and City Hall during Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann on Monday. The youth engagement manager at Oh Yeah, Chelsea Andrews said it was "amazing" that Sheeran was backing grassroots music in the cities.

Sheeran has previously spoken about the importance of support from his school music teacher when he was starting out.

His foundation is aims to support the teaching of music and increase opportunities for young musicians.

The singer-songwriter's father is from Belfast.

Sheeran previously visited the city to meet young rappers and performers after the launch of his foundation in the rest of the UK.

But he is now formally expanding its work into Northern Ireland and Ireland by funding North South Sounds 2026.

In a statement to BBC News NI, Sheeran said that Ireland was a "special" place for him.

"Every child should have the opportunity to learn and take part in music, and we're continuing our work to help make that a reality," Sheeran said.

"The first project kicks off at the Fleadh on Monday," he said.

"I played the festival last year and have such fond memories of it. If you're there, go and check out some of the incredible young talent."

Sheeran played a surprise gig in a pub during the 2025 Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann in Wexford.

Chelsea Andrews, who is also a singer and guitarist with the band GUSH, welcomed the move.

"A lot of musicians, no matter how good they are, we all experience that little bit of self-doubt sometimes," she said.

"So to have that other person, whether it be an unofficial mentor or a peer inspire you and encourage you and motivate you is really, really important."

She said there was a lot of excitement, and a little trepidation, about the Fleadh gig.

"Initially, it was 'Oh my goodness, this is so exciting,'"

"And then the realisation of 'Oh my goodness, this is a really big deal!'"

"But we are going to have them well prepared."

Musician Cheylene Murphy from the band Beauty Sleep has been leading the workshops with young people in Belfast.

"We've been getting them to improvise music together, they all met each other for the first time on Monday, we've been putting them in bands, we've been getting them to write new music based on a theme of what is Irish music to them?" she said.

"They're from lots of different genres and lots of different backgrounds and ranges.

"We've been trying to give them some performance advice and music industry advice, and every day we say 'How was today? What did you like? What didn't you like? What do you want to do tomorrow?

"After every day I go home and see if I can figure out a timetable to make that happen for them."

The Future Sounds of Belfast Showcase takes place at the Oh Yeah Centre on Monday 3 August from 14:00 BST.

articles.title: BBC cancels Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live at the Apollo
articles.text:
Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live at the Apollo have been cancelled by the BBC, as the corporation makes further financial savings.

The main Mastermind series will continue, with Clive Myrie remaining as host, but the celebrity spin-off will end after the next series, which has already been filmed.

In a statement, the BBC said it was "incredibly proud of all three of these much-loved shows" and thanked the programmes' production teams.

"Unfortunately," it continued, "we have to make some really tough choices in light of our funding challenges, and these savings have been identified from the Entertainment genre."

Viewing figures for all three shows have fallen over recent years. Celebrity Mastermind has dropped from an average of 4m viewers in 2017, to 1.7m for its most recent series.

Blankety Blank, meanwhile, has gone down from 5.5m viewers in 2021 to 2.3m for the most recent series.

And Live at the Apollo has dropped from around 1.3m viewers in 2018 to around 660,000 on its most recent series. These figures include catch-up platforms such as iPlayer.

Live at the Apollo, which has been running since 2004, also has one further series already filmed, but will not continue after that has been broadcast.

The show is normally anchored by a well-known comedian, who introduces two other comics to present their own stand-up routines at London's Hammersmith Apollo.

The programme has acted as a springboard for emerging comedy talent, and helped boost the early careers of Michael McIntyre, Kevin Bridges, Micky Flanagan and Sarah Millican.

Although Live at the Apollo will end, the BBC said it would "shortly be announcing digital plans focused on stand-up and emerging comedy talent".

They said the ongoing pivot to digital would "ensure we continue to support the stand-up community in a rapidly changing and increasingly competitive media landscape".

Celebrity Mastermind, which is filmed in Belfast, launched in 2002 and has also been presented by Magnus Magnusson and John Humphrys.

It was a spin-off from the main Mastermind series that launched three decades earlier and saw members of the public answer questions on general knowledge as well as a specialist subject.

The BBC said: "We will still continue to commission ambitious Entertainment shows and invest in distinctive UK content from a wide range of independent production companies of all sizes."

The corporation also said it would "prioritise digital innovation that can serve fans of these shows and beyond".

articles.title: Glen Hansard: Meeting heroes and the tape that changed his life
articles.text:
The death of Oscar-winning singer-songwriter Glen Hansard in a motorbike crash in Dublin on Wednesday has been met with widespread shock and grief.

The 56 year old, who shot to prominence when he was cast in 1991 musical comedy film The Commitments, was long-time frontman of rock band The Frames.

From Bono to Bruce Springsteen, tributes have poured in from around the world with friends and fans sharing stories about his life and the impact he made.

His was a life in music, from first picking up a guitar as a teenager right up until the final hours of his life, when he was performing in a traditional music session, external.

Here's a look of some of the remarkable aspects of his life in music and film.

It all started with a guitar and a cassette tape.

In an interview with Irish broadcaster RTÉ in February, external, Hansard said he learned to play the guitar as a child after one was left in his home by an uncle who had gone to prison.

Ballymun was one of Dublin's most economically deprived areas in the 1980s, hit hard by unemployment, crime and drug addiction.

"I was on a kind of a trajectory of getting into the drugs - only gently - getting heavy into drinking, very young, beginning to kind of break into things, just getting into that slightly dodgy spot," Hansard said.

But a Bob Dylan cassette, given to him by his girlfriend's brother, changed the path of his life.

"I listened to Bob Dylan and everything, like my whole world just went into the opposite - flipped," he said.

"I stayed in the bedroom, I played Bob Dylan songs every day, I learned my craft, I decided music was all I cared about.

"So that was a real turnaround for me, it was a life changer and I suddenly had my path."

He said he was also fortunate that his headmaster at school encouraged him down the path of music.

Hansard said he told him: "I can't guarantee you'll be famous, but if you start now, then you'll always be able to live from your guitar."

He left school at 13, and went on to form The Frames and sign his first record deal in 1990, the same year he became part of the cast of The Commitments.

It's odd to say about someone who was a musician through and through, but - whether by fate or accident - Hansard ended up appearing in two of the biggest films in Ireland's history.

Alan Parker's 1991 film, The Commitments, tells the story of the rise and fall of a soul band made up of young working-class Dubliners.

Hansard played the role of guitarist Outspan Foster, despite not originally auditioning for the part.

"I just showed up with my friend, we had been up all night," he told the XS Noize podcast earlier this year.

"He went for the audition and I sat outside waiting for him."

Hansard said they were about to leave when he was asked if he wanted to read for a part.

"They said you've got red hair, you play guitar, you fit the bill for this character that we're casting.

"So I went in and I read a few lines and I'd no problem with the accent because I'm from the north side of Dublin - so I'm a northsider, I play guitar and I've got red hair, I kind of fit the bill.

"So they gave me a callback and much to my surprise I got the part."

The film was an unlikely hit, going on to achieve cult status.

He described the experience as "incredible, it was a beautiful experience".

"It's sad for me that people have said to me 'I've heard you didn't enjoy the experience with The Commitments' - I loved it, I had an absolute ball.

"I just sort of felt it didn't define me and that was my little bit of resistance."

Incredibly, the reluctant actor went on to star in another seminal Irish film.

Hansard won his Oscar for the song Falling Slowly from the 2007 film Once, which he co-wrote with his co-star Markéta Irglova.

Again, it was a role he wasn't originally assigned to play.

Director John Carney had earmarked Irish actor Cillian Murphy for the role.

"He's quite a good singer. I thought I'd do the usual thing where you get a good actor who can half sing and train that voice, but then it became clear to everybody on the film that we should do it the other way around," Carney said in an interview with American film news website CHUD.

"We should get somebody who could really sing and half act and I'll trust that I would be able to do something magical with that."

He turned to his friend Hansard, who had co-written the music for the film.

As well as Bob Dylan - who he would meet a number of times - another of Hansard's musical heroes was Belfast's Van Morrison.

Hansard said his first meeting with Morrison was a rather awkward one when he was 19 or 20 at the star's birthday party at a member of the Guinness family's home.

As Morrison jammed in the kitchen, Hansard said his request for one of his songs was met with a gruff response from Morrison.

Later, at his friend's urging, Morrison passed his guitar to Hansard to play then promptly walked out of the room.

"I'm thinking 'the only guy I want to actually sing to is gone'," Hansard told Kevin Pollak's Chat Show.

Morrison returned during Hansard's second song and then asked the Dubliner to play the song he had requested earlier, before joining in singing it.

The two then went upstairs and took turns playing their songs to each other.

"I'm getting to sit and observe a master at work up close," Hansard said.

"We passed the guitar back and forth and I ran out of songs after an hour and a half and Van kept going and going."

He said as Morrison was leaving at the end of their jam session he said: "Nice voice, nice songs, blah, blah, blah."

Speaking to BBC's Radio Ulster in 2023 Hansard talked about meeting other legendary musical figures.

"Up in the high sweet air of that universe, it's very small and there's very few people and they're all making contact with each other," he said.

"For example, I was at some of [Pearl Jam singer] Eddie [Vedder's] sessions that were happening in Los Angeles and Ringo [Starr] came in and played drums, Stevie Wonder came in and played drums.

"Morrissey dropped in at one point and Iggy Pop dropped in.

"There's just this kind of place where there's never a question of how can I get that guy's phone number - everybody up at that level seems to have each other's contacts."

In the same interview, Hansard said his mother was a huge Beatles fan and came very close to meeting her heroes in the early 1960s.

"My mother climbed into the back of the Adelphi Cinema in Dublin - her and two of her mates - to see the Beatles," he said.

"They managed to get into the Beatles dressing room, they didn't know they were getting into the dressing room.

"And apparently they got up the corridor and [John] Lennon said: 'Hey mate, there's three more over here' and the girls all got kicked out.

"She always dined out on this story and she always called Paul McCartney Paul McCarty. But she adored The Beatles."

For the past 15 years, Hansard had organised an annual Christmas Eve busking gig to raise money for homelessness charities.

He persuaded many Irish stars, including Sinead O'Connor and members of U2, to join him in busking for cash in central Dublin.

Pat Green, of the Simon Community said the busk became "a tradition on the calendar" in the city.

He told BBC News NI's Good Morning Ulster programme on Thursday that Hansard had been motivated by a "sense of guilt and shame" during a city centre shopping trip at Christmas 2009.

"He was walking down Grafton Street himself with bags of presents and he passed a group of carol singers singing for the homeless and the Simon Community and they asked him to join in," Green explained.

"And he was busy, he was distracted and he said: 'No, I can't.'

"And he got home and it was then he realised there was no material value to the Christmas presents that he bought - that the greater value was out on the street, bringing joy and happiness to people over Christmas.

"So, he went back out and started to busk with literally the cap on the ground."

He said Hansard and other stars "have raised collectively – with Glen the leader – well over €2m (£1.7m) for homeless services that we provide here in Dublin's Simon."

Billy McGuinness, a guitarist in the Irish rock band Aslan, explained how Hansard was able to call in so many favours from his famous friends.

"Glen had this magical way of getting you to do something without making it feel like a job - he made you feel a part of it."

McGuinness also told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme that the singer was renowned for his kindness both on and off stage.

He cited the example of a young musician who had supported Hansard at a recent gig in County Cork.

"After the gig, Glen gave him a Takamine guitar and I believe that's not the first time that he did something like that," McGuinness said.

"That was the type of generous guy that he was."

Hansard was a long-time friend of Shane MacGowan, the late lead singer of the The Pogues.

Following MacGowan's death in 2023, MacGowan's widow Victoria Mary Clarke entrusted Hansard with the role of "musical director" of her husband's funeral.

Speaking to the Irish radio station Today FM, external on Wednesday, Clarke recalled how their friend stepped in to help.

"I said: 'Glen, would you be able to do something at the funeral?" she recalled.

"And he said: 'Look, if you don't mind, I'll do everything. I'll organise, I'll get all the music together, you don't have to worry.'"

MacGowan's send-off featured performances from Australian singer Nick Cave as well as a 'who's who' from the Irish music scene, including singer-songwriters Imelda May, Declan O'Rourke and Mundy, Hothouse Flowers frontman Liam Ó Maonlaí and Hansard's own band The Frames.

There were also readings from actor Johnny Depp, U2 singer Bono, Boomtown Rats singer Bob Geldoff and Irish actor Aidan Gillen.

"As people who watched it will testify, he did an incredible job, absolutely incredible, and in a short space – 24 hours – he pulled that together," Clarke said.

articles.title: BTS are back: return of K-pop superstars sparks US economic boom
articles.text:
BTS’s “Army” fanbase is descending on New York this weekend as the K-pop supergroup continues their first world tour after a four-year hiatus, sparking an economic boom wherever they land.

After shows in South Korea and Europe, the group are back in North America, with 14 shows in six US cities in August and September.

Following the rollout of BTS’s sixth album, Arirang, in March, fans have proved they are willing to spend. In Las Vegas, concertgoers who attended four sold-out shows in May generated an estimated $340m in economic activity, with events at huge hotels on the strip and at tiny Chinatown cafes.

HYBE, the group’s label, has partnered with local businesses and cultural centers for the “BTS The City – Arirang” project in select cities, offering exclusive BTS programming for concertgoers.

Ahead of two concerts at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium on 1 and 2 August, fans can follow a map of activities, landmarks and eateries that celebrate the group.

Manhattan’s Koreatown is bracing for thousands of fans. The economic impact of BTS concertgoers is expected to match that of soccer fans who crowded MetLife Stadium for the World Cup final – which included a BTS performance – a few weeks ago.

BTS will “easily compare [to] or even exceed Fifa’s economic impact just on average spending”, said Michael Mariano, head of economic development at Tourism Economics.

The group’s return has been a boon for HYBE, which reported a record-high revenue of $993m this past quarter.

The Korean Cultural Center New York will serve as the hub for fan activities. Participants who nabbed a coveted reservation can try on K-beauty products, sample desserts from Tous les Jours, a South Korean bakery chain, and customize the light sticks they’ll bring to the concert, known as “Army bombs”.

“K-pop can serve as a gateway to learning the Korean language and discovering Korean beauty, food, technology, tourism and other aspects of Korean culture,” said Bora Yoon, visual arts manager at the center.

The Arte Museum, which houses large-scale digital art, is hosting a special BTS exhibit that will feature music and digital art celebrating the group’s music. The museum expects a high demand for the exhibit, which will immerse BTS fans in “all five senses”, said Sang Jin Lee, head of the creative team and vice-president of d’strict, a creative design company that owns the Arte Museum.

“It’s about sharing our culture, great heritage and Korean contemporary digital art through the lens of BTS, using an enduring folk song that is continually reinterpreted by every generation,” Lee said in Korean, referring to Arirang, the centuries-old folk song that inspired the name of BTS’s new album.

New Wonjo, the oldest Korean barbecue restaurant in New York, is also featured on the map, and plans to serve a special menu inspired by the members of BTS and the foods they miss most on tour, including kimchi fried rice, pork belly and jajangmyeon, or black bean noodles.

The menu was developed “with intention, and is rooted in Korean culture, rather than just pasting ‘BTS’ on a regular menu item”, said Jacob Baik, art director of New Wonjo. “We hope that some guests who might initially visit because of the ‘BTS The City’ project leave with a genuine interest in the restaurant, the food and Korean culture more broadly.”

The map also features bingsu, a type of South Korean shaved ice dessert, offered by Seoul Bingsu – a pop-up version of Seoul-based Tokyo Bingsu, known for its tomato flavor of the dessert. For its limited 10-day New York run, Seoul Bingsu will offer special bookmarks, pins and stickers for those who order from its special Arirang menu.

Ara Go, the Seoul-based owner of Seoul Bingsu, said BTS “has truly helped introduce Korean culture to the world”.

“Food and desserts are a huge part of Korean culture, and I saw this as a wonderful opportunity to promote not only our food but our country with a broader audience,” Go said in Korean.

Before the spot’s collaboration with BTS, Angela May, 18, had never heard of bingsu. May, a BTS fan for nearly six years, traveled to Manhattan from New Jersey to try it.

“Just having BTS written on the menu or the window will bring a lot of attention to the place,” May said.

Asli Penaeo, 22, grew up in New York and has been a fan for seven years, yet she has never been to most of the collaborating restaurants.

“This event is finally giving me a chance to go to some of these restaurants, try new items, but also make new memories with fellow Army [fans],” she said, sipping on a BTS-branded Tous Les Jours strawberry lemonade.

Sunmi Lee, 40, an interior designer, said she was considering taking a BTS-themed double-decker bus tour to visit New York landmarks – even though she lives in the city.

“It’s about celebrating Korean culture,” she said. “Trying authentic local spots, and feeling connected to something bigger than just a concert.”

articles.title: ABC argues that early license review by FCC is ‘retaliation’ for network’s coverage
articles.text:
ABC has pushed back aggressively against the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for putting the network under an expedited license renewal process for eight local television stations it owns, charging in a lengthy filing that the process is payback for the network’s editorial decision-making and coverage of Donald Trump.

“The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country: Accommodate the administration’s view of what news coverage should look like or pay the price,” lawyers representing the Disney-owned network wrote in a 109-page filing, submitted as a reply to petitions from conservative media groups to deny ABC’s licenses. “The tools vary; the objective does not: a media industry too fearful of official reprisal to report the news freely.”

The FCC chair, Brendan Carr, has denied that inquiries into the network relate to its editorial decision-making and instead said they stem from concerns about the company’s employment practices and compliance with statutory obligations.

ABC’s lawyers pointed out how unusual it is for the FCC to demand that a group of network-owned stations apply several years early to renew their licenses. Other ABC-owned stations have licenses that run all the way until 2031.

“The commission’s departure from those norms lays bare what is really going on: the administration is retaliating against ABC for the exercise of its First Amendment rights,” ABC’s lawyers wrote. “Because this whole proceeding rests on an unconstitutional premise, the stations should never have been asked to justify license renewal years early.”

Responding to petitions to deny ABC’s licenses based on accusations of liberal bias, the network’s lawyers pointed out that the “commission has no authority to regulate the content of television programming”.

“No Petitioner has established any ‘violations’ of Commission rules or regulations, let alone the ‘serious’ ones or the ‘pattern of abuse’ required to warrant denying renewal,” they added.

ABC’s lawyers also argued that its eight stations had made “essential contributions to their local communities” in markets such as New York City and Philadelphia and argued that the FCC should dismiss the petitions to deny their licenses.

Participants have until 5 August to reply to petitions to deny. After that time, the FCC could choose to either grant the license renewal requests – an unlikely prospect – or schedule hearings on the matter, beginning a potentially onerous and time-consuming process that could run for several years, particularly if an adverse ruling is challenged in the courts.

On Tuesday, a bipartisan coalition of former FCC commissioners and staffers submitted a filing urging the commission to reject the petitions to deny ABC’s license renewals, arguing that the early renewal process ordered by Carr’s FCC in April is “a grave violation of both the Communications Act and the Constitution”.

Thousands of commenters have filed on behalf of ABC in both the license renewal inquiry and another FCC investigation into the daytime talkshow The View for a potential violation of rules guarding political candidate appearances.

“When given the chance to weigh in on whether to allow the FCC to continue its campaign of censorship and control, the American public showed up in a big way, and the vast majority who spoke up delivered the same message,” Anna M Gomez, the lone Democrat on the FCC, said in a statement on Thursday. “They believe in the value of their local news, they trust those who cover their communities, and they understand that the FCC has no business deciding who is a journalist and what counts as real news.”

articles.title: ‘Change is happening! I can cut off my hair and misbehave’: Vicky Krieps on rage, rebellion, and rejecting Hollywood
articles.text:
Back when she was a rising actor, Vicky Krieps had her fill of people telling her what not to do. When she got pregnant in her 20s, she was advised not to have the baby as it would derail her career, but she did it anyway. When, after playing a fashion designer’s muse in Paul Thomas Anderson’s Phantom Thread, she went back to making low-budget French films, she was, she says, “actually laughed at. It just seemed absurd to these people that I would turn my back on Hollywood and invest so much energy and passion in something that wasn’t giving me money.”

Yet Krieps’s determination to forge her own path has reaped rewards. For the last decade she has had one foot in the Hollywood mainstream, appearing in Fede Álvarez’s The Girl in the Spider’s Web and M Night Shyamalan’s Old, while keeping the other firmly in independent cinema where she has freedom to experiment. Krieps also does her utmost to avoid the pantomime of red-carpet events. On the occasions she does make an appearance, she will stick out her tongue or give photographers the finger. “I always smile when I’m doing it. But I’m telling them: ‘Guys, this is really ridiculous and the shouting is a bit much. Just talk nicely to me.’”

It comes as no surprise to learn that Krieps, 42, who was born and raised in Luxembourg and speaks four languages, has declined to make the obligatory move to Los Angeles. For the past 15 years, she has lived in Berlin – though, when we speak over video call, she is in Greece, which she regularly visits since marrying her husband, the Greek film production assistant Lazaros Gounaridis, last year. (They met on the set of the 2023 film Hot Milk.)

Sporting a pixie cut and a crisp white shirt, Krieps is open, thoughtful and speaks with unusual seriousness and candour about her job which, for her, is all-consuming. “Sometimes I feel less like an actor and more like a scientist who is experimenting on my own body,” she says.

This immersive approach can take a toll. Two weeks after wrapping her forthcoming film Love Me Tender, in which she plays a woman who loses custody of her young son, Krieps began feeling “really bad in my body. I was lying on my bed, and I couldn’t move my arms and my neck. I thought I had a serious disease.” She saw doctors and had an MRI, and found everything was fine but the pain itself was real. “I think I had assembled so much psychological pain that it became physical. You know the saying ‘My heart is aching’? I feel that in my whole chest.”

Directed by Anna Cazenave Cambet and based on the autobiographical novel by Constance Debré, Love Me Tender challenges the unfair expectations foisted upon mothers. Krieps plays Clémence, who has given up a well-paid legal career to write books. After separating amicably from her husband, Laurent, she gives away most of her belongings, immerses herself in the club scene and explores her sexuality. When she eventually tells Laurent that she is dating women, he appears to accept it. But afterwards, he makes dark allegations about her and questions her mental stability in a bid to secure sole custody of their eight-year-old son, Paul.

“Laurent,” says Krieps, “is an example of when the male ego starts to rage because it is hurting and doesn’t understand what is happening. He’s thinking: ‘Why am I not included in this? Why did this train leave without me?’” When “there is no real dialogue between men and women, men like this can become mean, sour and self-righteous”.

As their case creaks through the courts, Clémence is denied permission to see Paul. When they finally meet after nearly 18 months apart, it’s for an hour every fortnight under supervision. Those meetings, where Clémence must hold in her grief and keep it together for her son, are devastating. The tension of those scenes, Krieps realised, “caused me to hit a wall. But it was good for me to learn that the next time I work on something like this I will need to look after myself and take longer breaks while filming.”

Krieps has spent much of her career playing women trying to break out of the boxes that others have put them in. In Phantom Thread, she is Alma, a serving maid who is expected to remain meek in front of Daniel Day-Lewis’s dictatorial dressmaker but instead stands her ground and answers back. In 2022’s terrific Corsage, she is Elisabeth, Empress of Austria, celebrated in the 19th century for her beauty and her tiny waist (made tinier by ruthless corsetry), who rebels against her tightly controlled existence. In Emily Atef’s More Than Ever, she is a terminally ill woman fighting for the right to live out her days on her own terms.

“I talked to Charlotte Rampling about this after we worked on the Jim Jarmusch movie Father Mother Sister Brother,” Krieps reflects. “We realised what we have in common is that we are constantly drawn to exploring the edge of a [character], the place where it starts to hurt. I think I take this to every part.”

Where possible, Krieps tries to work with female directors – or rather, she clarifies, directors who preside over “feminine sets. I’ve worked with men where the set was not masculine and there was no male ego. And there are female directors who unfortunately operate with a male ego. A lot of film sets are run like the military and are very hierarchy-driven. It’s incredibly loud and it’s about pushing. But take a director like [Corsage’s] Marie Kreutzer: her set is extremely quiet and calm. No one is shouting. And the positive side to that is when you create silence, you start hearing each other.”

Picking apart societal roles and rejecting authority is in Krieps’s blood. Her grandfather was in the resistance during the second world war and survived internment at Dachau. He later became a socialist politician in Luxembourg and successfully mounted a campaign to abolish the death penalty. “Knowing that someone so close almost lost his life to fight for humanity, this is something you can’t forget,” reflects Krieps. Meanwhile, her mother “is just a crazy hippy, in the best way, and raised me to question everything: how do I know this is what they say it is? I think this made me dare to be brave and risk my livelihood.”

That daring surfaced when a teenage Krieps attended her school graduation ceremony and thanked her teachers for giving her “proof that I know how to learn off by heart, that I know how to copy and how to shut my mouth”. The incident made the papers in Luxembourg. It is also evident in her habit of tweaking the words and actions of her characters mid-scene. In Corsage, she launched herself out of a window in frustration at her onscreen husband (she emerged unscathed; the scene was filmed on the ground floor). The moment was not in the script but nonetheless made the final cut, with Krieps’s character sustaining a fracture from the fall. “These things are not premeditated but sometimes you just feel something that feels like the truth, and it wants to come out,” Krieps says.

True to her straddling of popular and arthouse entertainment, this autumn Krieps can be seen in Ryan Murphy’s series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story playing the Borden family’s maid Bridget Sullivan. She has also just finished work on Emma Doucet, a film by the French director Élise Girard about a single mother who falls in love with the French prime minister and which, she says, is “close to a poem. It’s very nouvelle vague.”

Krieps acknowledges that her questing spirit and single-mindedness as an actor wouldn’t have been possible even 20 years ago. “You wouldn’t have a woman who’s allowed to do all these different movies, and not give a fuck, cut off her hair and generally misbehave. The fact that I exist shows me change is happening and is possible.”

Love Me Tender is in UK and Irish cinemas from 7 August.
